title: The cold case
subtitle: Thermal conductors, insulators and a delivery problem
objective: Use evidence to explain thermal conduction and select insulation for a cold container.

sow.exactOutcome: Investigate thermal and electrical conductors and insulators.
sow.alignment: Directly develops the stated science outcome. Original secondary-age exemplar activities; diagnostic-led support and stretch follow the SoW. No claim of qualification approval.

priorLearning: Identify common materials and compare a measured temperature.
Use higher/lower and read whole-number values in a table.
success: Show the direction of energy transfer between warmer and cooler objects.
Explain why a thermal conductor transfers energy more readily than an insulator.
Choose an insulation jacket using two numbers and identify one test limitation.

vocabulary.meaning: Energy transfer through a material, or between touching materials, because of a temperature difference.
A material that transfers energy by conduction readily.
A material that transfers energy by conduction less readily.
Observations or measurements that help us judge a claim.

equipment: Printed evidence cards and one selected response route per pupil; pencils; optional calculator.
Optional teacher demonstration: smooth metal and wooden blocks kept in the room; contact thermometer.
No hot water, heater, ice handling or practical apparatus is needed for the complete lesson.
preparation: Print the common evidence page for every pair and choose response pages from the retrieval check.
If using the optional touch comparison, leave both safe samples in the same room well in advance and measure them before teaching.
Keep the constructed data visible. These are teaching examples, not results collected by this class.
safety: For the optional demonstration, use smooth, clean samples without sharp edges or splinters.
Touch is optional; pupils may observe temperature readings instead. Do not touch heated or chilled objects.
Use the complete paper route if safe sample preparation or supervision is unavailable.
practicalAlternative: The default route uses supplied diagrams and constructed evidence. It teaches the complete objective without handling hot or cold materials.

misconceptions.claim: Metal feels colder, so its temperature must be lower.
misconceptions.correction: Metal and wood can have the same temperature. A warmer hand loses energy faster to the better conductor.
misconceptions.check: Ask the pupil to compare both 20 °C labels before explaining the different feeling.

misconceptions.correction: Insulation slows energy transfer. It can slow warming of a cold object as well as cooling of a warm object.
misconceptions.check: Ask why the foam-jacketed cold bottle warms less.

misconceptions.claim: Cold moves out of the ice.
misconceptions.correction: Net energy transfer is from warmer surroundings towards colder ice.
misconceptions.check: Draw an arrow into the ice and name the warmer object.

misconceptions.claim: One result proves this material is always best.
misconceptions.correction: The result supports a conclusion about these jackets under these conditions. Thickness, fit and other conditions also matter.
misconceptions.check: Ask which feature would need controlling before comparing materials themselves.

access.supported: Use page 2 with arrow choices, the two most relevant table rows and a sentence frame. Adult reads the same science aloud. Pointing, drawing or dictated answers are valid.
access.standard: Use page 3 to calculate temperature rises and justify a design decision using comparative evidence.
access.stretch: Use page 4 to evaluate an unfair comparison and transfer the explanation to a warm container. Same thermal objective, deeper reasoning.
access.regulation: Offer silent think time, a seated evidence role, optional partner talk and a short pause. No speed contest or public reading requirement. Pupils may change route after the hinge.

sources.title: US Department of Energy: Heat Flow
sources.note: Checked 9 September 2026. Direction of conduction and distinction between transfer mechanisms; diagrams and tasks are original.

sources.title: NSW Government: Insulation

slides.title: Can a jacket keep something cold?
body: A cold drink must arrive cool.
Your job: choose a jacket and defend it with evidence.
Today: notice → explain → test the claim.
slides.notes: Introduce an ordinary cold-drink delivery, with no health or food-storage guarantee. The scientific decision concerns only temperature change over 20 minutes. Say: We can change our first idea when evidence improves it.

slides.title: What do we already know?
body: R1. Name the material in a metal spoon.
R2. Which is warmer: 8 °C or 20 °C?
R3. Name a tool that measures temperature.
slides.notes: Answers: a suitable metal such as steel; 20 °C; thermometer. Accept everyday language, then supply the scientific word. If values are confused, locate 8 and 20 on an imagined number line. Do not teach relative temperature by touching unknown objects.

slides.title: Feeling is not a thermometer
body: The samples both start at 20 °C.
A warmer hand loses energy to both.
Metal transfers that energy more quickly.
slides.notes: 8 minutes shared across this and the next two I do slides. Think aloud: I notice the two thermometer readings match. So lower starting temperature cannot explain the different feeling. I compare how quickly energy leaves the warmer hand. Optional smooth room-temperature sample observation only. The about-32 °C hand is an illustrative value, not a body-temperature claim.

visual.title: Same temperature; different feeling
visual.description: A warmer hand transfers energy to metal and wood at the same room temperature. A thicker arrow represents faster transfer into metal, not a lower starting temperature.

elements.text: Arrow width is a model, not measured data.

slides.title: Why can ice melt faster on metal?
body: Energy transfers from warmer to cooler objects.
A metal tray can transfer energy towards ice quickly.
Melting does not mean the tray started hotter.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Trace the arrows from tray towards ice. Conduction through metal helps supply energy for melting. Explain that energy also enters from air and radiation; the diagram isolates the contact route. Do not imply the tray stays at 20 °C throughout or that all metals behave identically.

visual.title: Energy can melt ice
visual.description: At room temperature, energy transfers from the warmer surroundings through the warmer tray towards the ice. Faster melting is evidence of faster energy transfer in this set-up; sizes are not to scale.

elements.text: Ice is cooler than the tray and room

Ice gains energy
and can melt
Model: other energy routes and sizes are simplified.

slides.title: Insulation changes the rate
body: Thermal insulators slow transfer by conduction.
A jacket can slow cooling or warming.
It does not create heat or stop transfer forever.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Model the cold case: 20 °C room is warmer than 8 °C contents, so energy transfers inwards. A foam jacket slows this. Trapped gas in foam reduces conduction and limits bulk air movement; do not claim conduction is the only route in a real bottle.

visual.title: An insulator slows transfer in either direction
visual.description: Two insulated containers: energy moves out from warm contents to a cooler room; energy moves in from a warmer room to cool contents. Insulation slows both transfers. Arrows show net energy transfer only.

elements.text: The green jacket adds insulation. It makes no heat.

slides.title: Evidence detectives: feeling versus measurement
body: D1. Both blocks measured 20 °C. Metal felt colder.
D2. In an ice test, more ice melted on metal.
Use page 1: reject, keep or improve each claim.
slides.notes: 8 minutes shared across three We do slides. Give pairs the common evidence page. Roles: evidence finder and claim editor, with silent individual alternative. D1 rejects metal must be colder. D2 is consistent with faster energy transfer through the metal set-up. It alone does not measure conductivity because dimensions, masses, contact and other routes affect melting.

slides.title: Which bottle warmed least?
body: Constructed sample data: identical sealed bottles.
All start at 8 °C in a 20 °C room.
Read the 20-minute temperature; justify one choice.
slides.notes: Shared We do time. Ask everyone to first point at the lowest final temperature. Compute rises together: 14−8=6 °C, 12−8=4 °C, 10−8=2 °C. The foam jacket performed best among these tested jackets. Table concerns a single model comparison; repeat before a stronger conclusion.

table.caption: Constructed sample data; equal bottles, fill, start temperature and room.

slides.title: Improve the delivery claim
body: Claim: “Foam makes cold and is always best.”
Replace it with a sentence the evidence supports.
Name one extra check before a bigger decision.
slides.notes: Shared We do time. Model after pupil attempts: In this test, the foam jacket limited warming to 2 °C, compared with 6 °C without a jacket. It slowed energy transfer into the bottle. Repeat tests; record thickness and fit; test longer journeys. Accept equivalent bounded conclusions.
slides.reveal: This foam jacket slowed warming most in this 20-minute test.

slides.title: A cold bottle wears an insulating jacket
body: The room is warmer than the bottle. What happens?
slides.notes: Take simultaneous responses by pointing, cards or private writing. If A or C chosen, revisit the cold-container arrow before independent work. If D chosen, ask which value remains lower than the room temperature.

options.feedback: No. A passive jacket does not produce cold; it slows energy transfer.

options.text: Energy still transfers in, but more slowly.
options.feedback: Yes. The room is warmer, so net energy transfer is inwards; insulation slows it.

options.text: The jacket stops all transfer forever.
options.feedback: No. Insulation reduces the rate; temperatures can still move towards room temperature.

options.text: Energy transfers from cold bottle to warmer room.
options.feedback: No. The net transfer in this situation is from the warmer room to the cooler bottle.

slides.title: Your design brief
body: Choose one response page: supported, standard or stretch.
Recommend a jacket using the common evidence.
Explain where energy moves and why.
slides.notes: 10 minutes shared across the three You do slides. All routes assess the same objective. Select after the hinge, not from a fixed ability label. Provide page 1 with each route. Read prompts aloud or scribe verbatim where needed. Independent explanation can be drawn and dictated.

slides.title: Make the evidence do the work
body: Name the two objects at different temperatures.
Use at least one pair of values.
Finish: “This shows … in this test.”
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Supported: 10 versus 14 °C and inward arrow suffice with a clear explanation. Standard: show all rises. Stretch: compare a thick foam sleeve with a thin cotton sleeve fairly, and explain warm-container transfer. Prompt with questions, not the conclusion.

slides.title: Check before you submit
body: Have I used “slows” rather than “stops”?
Does my arrow go from warmer to cooler?
Have I separated evidence from a guess?
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Teacher checks one explanation per pupil. For metal feels colder misconception, return to identical thermometer labels. For cold escapes, ask which object gives energy to which. Do not add new technical vocabulary during independent work.

slides.title: Compare and improve
body: Show one sentence or arrow you improved.
Check a partner’s evidence without judging their first idea.
What would make our conclusion stronger?
slides.notes: 4 minutes shared across two Review slides. Offer private teacher sharing. Listen for foam jacket slowed warming; 2 °C rather than 6 °C; repeat under controlled conditions. Praise a specific revision of reasoning rather than speed or confidence.

slides.title: Our evidence has a boundary
body: We compared three particular jackets.
Thickness, fit and repeat results still matter.
Pupil choice: which jacket variable should be tested next?
slides.notes: Shared Review time; light Lundy cycle. Invite a spoken, written or pointed proposal; teacher records one and explains which can be tested next, such as equal material at two thicknesses. Explain that listening led to a planned test, not merely collecting a vote. No obligation to disclose feelings.

slides.title: Three things to leave with
body: E1. Draw energy’s direction: room 20 °C, bottle 8 °C.
E2. Explain what a thermal insulator does.
E3. Give one number that supports the foam choice.
slides.notes: Answers: arrow room to bottle; slows energy transfer; 10 °C final or 2 °C rise, ideally compared with 14 °C or 6 °C unwrapped. Collect independent evidence; an adult may read and scribe without supplying concepts.

pupilPages.title: 1 • Shared evidence: the cold case
pupilPages.intro: Keep this page beside your chosen response route. All numerical examples below are constructed sample data, not observations from your class.

cards.title: D1 • Same room
cards.text: Smooth metal and wood blocks both measured 20 °C. A warmer hand felt the metal as colder.

cards.title: D2 • Melting clue
cards.text: Equal 20 g ice pieces, both starting at about 0 °C, sat on room-temperature trays. After 5 minutes: metal set-up 9 g melted; plastic set-up 3 g melted. Tray dimensions matched; masses differed.

cards.title: C1 • First claim
cards.text: “The metal must have started colder because it felt colder.”

cards.title: C2 • Second claim
cards.text: “The metal set-up transferred energy to the ice faster in this test.”

cards.title: C3 • Delivery claim
cards.text: “A foam jacket makes cold and is always the best jacket.”

blocks.text: Delivery test: constructed sample data. Identical sealed bottles, equal fill, same 20 °C room, all starting at 8 °C. Jackets fitted fully; jacket thickness was not matched.

blocks.prompt: W1. Which claims can you keep, reject or improve? Explain one using D1 or D2.
W2. Which jacket limited warming most? Name one check needed before claiming a material is always best.

pupilPages.title: 2 • Supported route: choose and explain
pupilPages.intro: Use page 1. Point, circle, draw or dictate; the science goal is the same.

blocks.prompt: S1. The bottle starts at 8 °C. The room is 20 °C. Which is warmer?
S2. Draw an energy arrow between ROOM and BOTTLE. Label the warmer end.
S3. Which final temperature shows the coldest bottle after 20 minutes?
S4. Complete: I choose ____ . It reached ____ °C, compared with ____ °C without a jacket. It ____ energy transfer into the bottle. Word bank: slows / stops forever.
S5. The two blocks were both 20 °C. Why did metal feel colder? Use: hand / energy / faster.
S6. Name or circle one useful next check: repeat the test / guess from jacket colour. Explain your choice.

pupilPages.title: 3 • Standard route: delivery recommendation
pupilPages.intro: Use page 1. The table repeats constructed sample data from page 1. Complete one evidence-backed decision for the delivery team.

blocks.prompt: N1. Draw and label the net energy-transfer direction between a 20 °C room and an 8 °C bottle.
N2. Complete the rises. Show one subtraction, then compare foam with no jacket.
N3. Recommend a jacket. Explain its effect on energy transfer using two numerical values.
N4. Explain why the 20 °C metal may feel colder than the 20 °C wood to a warmer hand.
N5. Give one limitation of the jacket evidence and one precise improvement.

pupilPages.title: 4 • Stretch route: challenge the claim
pupilPages.intro: Use page 1. Your task is to justify a useful decision without claiming more than the data show.

blocks.prompt: T1. Calculate all three temperature rises. Recommend a jacket and explain the direction and rate of energy transfer.

T2. The foam sleeve was 10 mm thick; the cotton sleeve was 2 mm thick. Constructed test details. Can this establish that foam material is better at every thickness? Explain and redesign this comparison.
T3. Now put 40 °C water inside an insulated bottle in the same 20 °C room. Draw energy’s direction and explain how the same jacket changes cooling. This is a thought experiment only.
T4. Evaluate: “The ice result proves conductivity alone caused the difference.” Use one limitation from D2 and propose one improvement.

pupilPages.title: 5 • Exit and scientific reflection
pupilPages.intro: Answer independently. A drawing or spoken response recorded by an adult is welcome.

blocks.prompt: E1. Room 20 °C; bottle 8 °C. Draw and label the net energy-transfer arrow.
E2. What does a thermal insulator do?
E3. Give numerical evidence for the foam-jacket recommendation from page 1.
E4. What extra measurement or comparison would you ask the class to investigate next?
Reflection. One idea I changed because of evidence was …

answers.label: R1–R3
answers.answer: R1: steel/stainless steel or another suitable metal. R2: 20 °C. R3: a thermometer. Re-teach reading temperature values if needed.

answers.label: W1 / C1
answers.answer: Reject C1. Both samples measured 20 °C. The warmer hand transfers energy to the metal faster, so feeling alone does not establish lower temperature.

answers.label: W1 / C2
answers.answer: Keep the bounded claim C2: more ice melted in the metal set-up in the same time (9 g versus 3 g), consistent with faster net energy transfer into the ice in this set-up. It does not isolate conductivity alone; tray masses differed and other energy routes exist.

answers.label: W1 / C3
answers.answer: Improve C3: the foam jacket slowed warming most in this test. It does not make cold and the test does not prove superiority under all conditions.

answers.label: W2
answers.answer: Foam: final 10 °C and rise 2 °C, versus no jacket 14 °C and rise 6 °C. Useful checks include repeated trials; matched thickness if comparing material properties; matched jacket fit; a longer journey test.

answers.label: Hinge A–D
answers.answer: A incorrect: a passive insulator makes no cold. B correct: net transfer is into the colder bottle and is slower with insulation. C incorrect: it does not stop transfer forever. D incorrect: direction is warmer room to cooler bottle. Use the cold-container diagram if A, C or D persist.

answers.label: S1–S3
answers.answer: S1 room. S2 arrow from ROOM (20 °C, warmer) towards BOTTLE (8 °C, cooler). S3 foam at 10 °C.

answers.label: S4–S6
answers.answer: S4 foam; 10; 14; slows. S5 the warmer hand loses energy faster to metal although both blocks begin at the same temperature. S6 repeat the test, to check whether the pattern happens again. Colour alone does not establish this performance.

answers.label: N1–N2
answers.answer: N1 room to bottle. N2 none: 14−8=6 °C; cotton: 12−8=4 °C; foam: 10−8=2 °C. Foam warmed 4 °C less than no jacket over the same interval.

answers.label: N3–N5
answers.answer: N3 recommend this foam sleeve: it slowed energy transfer in from the warmer room, with only a 2 °C rise compared with 6 °C unwrapped. N4 both are 20 °C; metal conducts energy away from the warmer hand faster. N5 one set of results lacks repeat confidence; repeat each test. Thickness was not matched; match it to compare material properties. Check and report fit carefully too. Accept other specific, relevant control improvements.

answers.label: T1–T2
answers.answer: T1 rises 6, 4 and 2 °C. Recommend foam for this brief; energy enters from the warmer room, more slowly with the jacket. T2 no: thickness changed as well as material. Compare equal-thickness, equal-coverage jackets with identical bottles, starting values and conditions; repeat. This tests those equal-thickness samples, not every possible design.

answers.label: T3–T4
answers.answer: T3 arrow from 40 °C contents to 20 °C room; insulation slows energy loss so the contents cool more slowly. No physical hot-water method is requested. T4 the evidence compares full tray set-ups, not conductivity alone. Tray masses differed; use matching dimensions, control initial temperatures and contact, document masses and repeat. Even then, heat capacity and other transfer routes require care before attributing the effect solely to conductivity.

answers.label: E1–E4
answers.answer: E1 room to bottle. E2 slows energy transfer by conduction; accept a correctly explained broader slows heat transfer. E3 foam 10 °C or 2 °C rise; stronger evidence compares 14 °C or 6 °C unwrapped. E4 a testable suggestion such as same material at two thicknesses, repeated trials, or a longer fixed duration. Reflection has no prescribed opinion; assess connection to evidence.

answers.label: Assessment / re-teach
answers.answer: Secure objective: correct warmer-to-cooler arrow, explains an insulator slows transfer, and numerical recommendation bounded to this test. A correct choice without an explanation is emerging evidence. For cold moves or jackets make heat, narrate the two-temperature diagram, then ask a new cold-lunchbox example. For overclaiming, underline in this test and ask for one missing control.

teacherNotes: Timing totals 40 minutes: opening 2; retrieval 3; I do 8; We do 8; hinge 3; independent 10; review/Lundy 4; exit 2. Zero-minute slides share their stage allocation.
Default lesson is an evidence investigation. Do not imply that pupils performed the constructed experiments. Optional tactile demonstration is only at room temperature.
Use pathway support flexibly. The objective stays scientific reasoning about thermal transfer; reading, writing and social participation can be adjusted independently.

Diagrams are selective models: arrows represent net energy transfer, not a substance called cold. The ice drawing omits other energy pathways, and the bottle model simplifies thickness, fit, air movement and radiation.

Cover script: read the two temperature values first; say which is warmer; trace energy’s direction; explain what changes the rate; then compare measured outcomes. Each step is one question before giving the worked explanation.
